teaser: Six years of work, a neck like a swan's, and a painting its maker never finished.

lesson.text: Around 1917 in Paris, Amedeo Modigliani painted women with necks like flower stems and faces like long ovals, and people called it modern. The recipe was almost four hundred years old. A young painter from Parma had already stretched a woman far past nature, and he did it on a church altarpiece.

His name was Girolamo Francesco Mazzola, known as Parmigianino, “the little one from Parma.” In 1534 a noblewoman, Elena Baiardi, ordered a Virgin and Child from him for her family chapel. He was to deliver it within months. He was still working on it when he died, six years later.

The panel is tall, about 2.16 meters (7 feet). Mary sits high above you with the sleeping Christ Child across her lap, and a crowd of young angels presses in from the left. Nothing here is wrong by accident. Each stretch is a decision, and you can trace them.

lesson.title: Stretched on purpose
lesson.text: Four places where the body has been pulled longer than any real body.

spots.title: The neck
spots.text: The detail that named the painting. It rises like a pale column from the shoulders, and the small tilted head on top makes it seem longer still.

spots.title: The hand
spots.text: Fingers as thin as candles rest on her chest, barely pressing the cloth. Hands like these became a signature of elegant painting for the next fifty years.

spots.title: The child
spots.text: He is far too large for a baby, limp, pale and sliding off her knees. The dangling arm recalls images of the dead Christ in his mother's lap. His sleep is a forecast.

spots.title: An angel's leg
spots.text: One long bare leg runs up the left edge, polished like ivory. It belongs to the angel holding the vase, and it works as a matching pillar on this side.

lesson.text: Art historians call this taste Mannerism, from the Italian maniera, meaning style. After Raphael and Michelangelo had mastered natural bodies, a younger generation asked what came next. Their answer: grace pushed beyond nature, so that elegance itself becomes the subject.

Parmigianino announced his love of distortion at about twenty-one. He painted his own reflection in a barber's convex mirror, on a curved piece of wood, with his hand ballooning in the foreground. He carried it to Rome as a calling card for the pope.
If the figures are bent, the picture as a whole is not. It stands on a few firm lines, and one of them explains why the neck looks the way it does.
Three lines hold the stretched bodies together.

lines.label: The serpentine
lines.text: From her hair to her bare toes on the cushion, Mary's body winds in a slow S. Painters of the time prized this twisting line as the shape of grace.

lines.label: The column
lines.text: A smooth white column climbs behind her, the same color and the same roundness as her neck. An old hymn compared the Virgin's neck to a column, and the painter shows it literally.

lines.label: The child's slide
lines.text: The baby lies on a slope running down to the left, toward the angels. With nothing to stop him, he seems about to slip out of the picture.

lesson.text: That column is odd, though. It holds up nothing: no roof, no arch, only sky. And at its foot the scale collapses. Something very small is standing down there.
A man no taller than the Virgin's shin is unrolling a scroll. Where is he?

spots.title: Saint Jerome
spots.text: A gaunt, half-naked man holds up a scroll in the lower right corner. He is Saint Jerome, the scholar who translated the Bible into Latin. He stands far away, which makes the space behind Mary feel dizzyingly deep.

lesson.text: Jerome was supposed to have company. Next to his feet, at the very edge, floats a single painted foot. It is all that exists of a second saint. The sky above is only brushed in, and behind the big column a row of others is hinted at and abandoned. The painting simply stops.

According to the biographer Giorgio Vasari, Parmigianino spent his last years obsessed with alchemy, trying to turn mercury into gold, and let his commissions rot. In 1539 he was even jailed for failing to finish frescoes in another Parma church.

He died in 1540, at thirty-seven. Two years later the panel was hung in the chapel as it was, with a Latin line added on the step under the column: fate prevented him from completing it. Faint traces of the lettering can still be seen there.
Mannerism trades natural proportions for elegance. Here a long neck is not a mistake but a claim: beauty can be invented, not just copied.

In 1698 a Medici prince bought the altarpiece and took it to Florence, where it still hangs. Visitors keep giving it nicknames, most of them about the neck. Nobody remembers what Elena Baiardi wanted to call it.

The angel at the far left holds a tall, slender vase with a shape that rhymes with the long leg beside it. On its curved belly some viewers have made out the faint image of a cross, one more hint of what awaits the sleeping child.

quiz.question: Who commissioned the painting?
options: Elena Baiardi, for her family chapel in Parma
quiz.explanation: Elena Baiardi ordered it in 1534 for her chapel; the Medici bought it much later.

quiz.question: What does the word Mannerism come from?
quiz.explanation: Maniera means style: elegance pushed beyond nature.

quiz.question: Who is the tiny man with the scroll?
quiz.explanation: He is Saint Jerome, translator of the Bible into Latin.

quiz.question: What remains of the second saint who was meant to stand beside him?
quiz.explanation: Only one painted foot exists at the edge, a sign the work was left unfinished.

quiz.question: Why does the sleeping child look unsettling?
options: His limp, pale body recalls the dead Christ on his mother's lap
quiz.explanation: His dangling arm and pallor echo images of the dead Christ.

facts.text: Parmigianino finished the painting a few months after it was ordered.
facts.explanation: He worked on it for six years and left it unfinished when he died in 1540.

facts.text: The white column behind Mary supports nothing.
facts.explanation: It rises into empty sky, with no roof or arch above it.

facts.text: The painting has always been in Florence.
facts.explanation: It was made for a chapel in Parma and bought by a Medici prince only in 1698.
